name: The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law
title: The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law
answer: This idea covers three newer rule sets that affect schools: accessibility standards for district websites and digital tools, federal limits on deepfake intimate images, and state student privacy and AI laws. It matters because districts must update their websites, handbooks, reporting routes, and staff training, and because state rules can add obligations beyond federal law. The text frames these as compliance duties that schools should confirm with counsel where needed.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The newer rules add accessibility, deepfake, and state law duties to the privacy and safety work schools already do. The accessibility rule requires public school districts to make websites, online forms, learning platform content, and apps meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. The deepfake rule makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish intimate images of a person without consent, including images made by AI, with higher penalties when the victim is a minor. State laws often go further than federal law, and many regulate education companies directly. The problem these rules solve is that older policies may not cover digital access, AI-generated abuse, or state-specific privacy and AI governance.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give grade bands, so the work applies across a district rather than to one age group. Districts should update handbooks, reporting steps, and staff training so a student who is targeted knows exactly where to go. For accessibility, public school districts must bring websites, online forms, learning platform content, and apps to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, with deadlines after an April 2026 extension: April 26, 2027 for areas of 50,000 or more people and April 26, 2028 for smaller districts. For deepfakes, covered platforms must remove reported images within 48 hours since May 19, 2026. For state law, Ohio requires every district to adopt an AI policy, and Texas districts should confirm their obligations with counsel under a law that took effect in January 2026.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no research evidence label and no study findings. It cites legal and policy sources: THE Journal, 2026 for the accessibility deadlines and the court challenge; Latham & Watkins, 2025 for the TAKE IT DOWN Act; ManagedMethods, n.d. for the figure that at least 40 states had passed student privacy laws by 2019; and Texas Legislature, 2025 for the Texas AI governance law. The text also states that most states have issued guidance on AI in schools and that Ohio now requires every district to adopt an AI policy. Because the text offers no research evidence, this idea rests on practice and legal requirements rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets several limits. The accessibility extension is being challenged in court, so the deadlines may not be final. State law often goes further than federal law, and many states regulate education companies directly, so district obligations can vary. Texas districts should confirm their obligations with counsel because the Texas AI governance law defines covered government entities broadly enough to include school districts. Decisions stay with people: schools should update handbooks, reporting steps, and staff training, and a student who is targeted should know exactly where to go. The text does not give legal advice, and districts should treat these as practice and compliance matters to verify with counsel.
